seo.meta_title: '저희 나라' or '우리나라'? | The Humble Form AI Overuses
seo.meta_description: AI often makes 'our country' extra polite as '저희 나라' — but Koreans say '우리나라' even in formal speech. Here's why.

ai_failure.situation: Politely telling a Korean person something about Korea, e.g. 'In our country, we eat rice cake soup on New Year's.'
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Uses '저희 나라' because 저희 is the humble form of 'we/our' and the sentence is polite.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: When Koreans talk about Korea, 저희 나라 humbles the nation itself. To a Korean listener that makes no sense, since they belong to the same country, and there's no reason to lower your country in front of foreigners either. Standard guidance from the National Institute of Korean Language treats 우리나라 as correct in every register, whoever the listener is.

natural_solution.rule: Koreans say 우리나라 (or 한국) for Korea in every register, to Koreans and foreigners alike. Learners talking about their own country: use the country's name, or 우리 나라 with a space. Written as one word, 우리나라 means Korea. Use 저희 for groups the listener is not part of: your company, your family, your team.

alternatives.context: A Korean talking about Korea, to anyone
A learner talking about their own country — naming it is clearest

alternatives.phrase: 우리 나라에서는 크리스마스가 제일 큰 명절이에요.
alternatives.romanization: u-ri na-ra-e-seo-neun keu-ri-seu-ma-seu-ga je-il keun myeong-jeo-ri-e-yo
alternatives.context: A learner's 'my country', with a space, so it isn't read as Korea
Correct use of 저희 — the listener isn't part of your company

nuance: 저희 lowers the speaker's group relative to the listener, so it only works when the listener stands outside that group. For Koreans, the nation isn't something to lower to anyone, so 우리나라 is written as a single word and used by presidents and news anchors alike. As one word it refers only to Korea, which is why a learner's 'my country' is safer as the country's name or 우리 나라 with a space. Learners do often say 저희 나라 about their own country to Koreans; it is heard as humble rather than wrong, but it isn't necessary. The trap shows how Korean politeness isn't a dial you simply turn up — it depends on who is inside and who is outside the 'we'.
